links.outcome: LLM annotation accuracy versus manual annotation ground truth for housing instability
links.effect: GPT-4 recall 0.924 vs human annotators 0.702; precision 0.850 vs 0.971; no evidence of hallucinations in GPT-4 outputs
links.quote: Compared with GPT-3.5 and the NER model, GPT-4 had the highest performance and had a much higher recall (0.924) than human annotators (0.702) in identifying patients experiencing current or past housing instability, although precision was lower (0.850) compared with human annotators (0.971).

links.outcome: Comparison of GPT-4 against GPT-3.5, NER model, RegEx and human annotators on same notes
links.effect: GPT-4 had the highest performance among automated methods and higher recall than humans (0.924 vs 0.702) but lower precision (0.850 vs 0.971).
links.quote: Compared with GPT-3.5 and the NER model, GPT-4 had the highest performance and had a much higher recall (0.924) than human annotators (0.702) in identifying patients experiencing current or past housing instability, although precision was lower (0.850) compared with human annotators (0.971).

unlisted_practices: Chain-of-thought prompting requiring evidence and justification to reduce hallucinations
Testing LLM performance on de-identified versus original clinical notes
Using LLMs for computer-assisted annotation with human review

screen.reason: The study evaluates GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 for extracting social determinants of health (housing instability) from clinical notes compared to manual annotation and NER, evaluating model extraction accuracy without comparing specific organizational deployment practices or safeguards.
